speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: TELEVISION
subtopic: PETITION REQUESTING PRIVATE STATION IN MUNICIPALITY OF BURNABY, B.C.
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the house that the Clerk has laid on the table the tenth report of the clerk of petitions. In connection with the petition referred to in this report, however, I received a memorandum from the Clerk which is to the following effect:
It is my duty to inform you that, although the petition presented by Mr. Goode on Wednesday last meets the requirements of Standing Order 70 as to form, it is irregular, in my opinion, on the grounds that it does not set forth a case in which the house has jurisdiction to interfere. See page 814 of May's Parliamentary Practice, 15th Edition.
This petition prays that this House may be pleased to take such measures as may be deemed expedient for the purpose of having the government of Canada and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation consider the advisability of permitting the establishment of a private television station in Burnaby, B.C.
By virtue of the Canadian Broadcasting Act, chapter 32. R.S.C., 1952 and of the Radio Act, chapter 233, R.S.C., 1952, Parliament has decided that licences to operate private television stations shall be issued by the Minister of Transport, with the approval of the Governor in Council. The relevant sections of the respective acts read as follows:
Section 22(1) of the Canadian Broadcasting Act: "The Minister of Transport shall before dealing with any application for licence to establish a new private station or for increase in power, change of channel, or change of location of any existing private station, or making any regulations or changes in regulations governing the activities of private stations, refer such application or regulation to the Corporation and the Corporation shall give public notice thereof in the Canada Gazette and shall make such recommendation to the Minister of Transport as it may deem fit; the approval of the Governor in Council shall be obtained before any licence for a new private station is issued."
Section 5(1) of the Radio Act:
"No person shall establish a radio station or private receiving station, or install, operate or have in his possession a radio apparatus at any place in Canada or on any aircraft registered in Canada, except under and in accordance with a licence granted by the Minister in that behalf."
It is my opinion that since Parliament has vested in the Governor in Council and in the Minister of Transport the exclusive authority to approve and issue licences for the operation of television stations, the House has no jurisdiction in such matters. See Citation 600 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, 3rd Edition.
Therefore, I maintain that according to the practice of this House, the petition should not be received.
I concur in the opinion given to me by the Clerk and therefore beg to inform the hon. member and the house that this petition cannot be received.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house may be interested to know that a further reduction in the commonwealth forces serving under the United Nations command in Korea has been decided upon.
In so far as this country is concerned the present Canadian component of some 300 officers and men will be reduced to a small detachment of about 40 personnel of the Royal Canadian Army Medical Corps and the Royal Canadian Dental Corps. They will continue to provide medical and dental facilities to all commonwealth troops in Korea.
Our reduction will be phased in with that of other commonwealth countries concerned. These withdrawals are to begin next month and are to be completed as soon as practicable thereafter.
The commonwealth force then remaining in Korea will include a British infantry battalion and supporting detachments from Canada, Australia and New Zealand. This force will be known as the commonwealth contingent, Korea, and will retain its identity under the United Nations command.

There is no answer I can give other than the answer I have given the hon. member on two or three occasions. The answer is that we offer 38 cents a dozen for grade A large eggs in storage at cold storage plants. If eggs are delivered there the prices board will of course make provision for storing the eggs subject to the fact that they

will take them over at 38 cents a dozen, if necessary, on December 1 next. But if the eggs are not delivered to a storage plant where they can be taken care of, of course the plan does not come into operation.

I am not at all certain whether or not the prices in the Star-Phoenix constitute breaking the floor, but there is a very simple way in which the floor price can be enforced. This government has no right to set the price for eggs in any province but we have the right to say that we will buy eggs at a particular price. We have said we will buy them at 38 cents in storage as of the 1st of December, and any provincial government can pass a law compelling the delivery of eggs on this basis without taking any chance of losing anything. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Hugues Lapointe (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: THE VICTORIA CROSS
subtopic: INVITATION TO CANADIAN HOLDERS TO PARTICIPATE IN ONE HUNDREDTH ANNIVERSARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on January 31 the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hosking) inquired from me whether the government was considering sending Canadian war heroes who had been awarded the Victoria Cross to attend the ceremonies that will mark the creation of that military award next June. At that time I stated that an interdepartmental committee had been set up to get the necessary information and that I would be in a position to make a further announcement later.
I wish now to say that the United Kingdom government has advised the government of Canada of the celebrations planned in June of this year to mark the centenary of the Victoria Cross decoration and has expressed the hope that Canadian holders of the Victoria Cross will be able to attend.
The ceremonies include a service in Westminster Abbey on the afternoon of June 25, a review by Her Majesty the Queen of all V.C. holders in Hyde Park on the morning of the 26th, and a garden party in the grounds of Marlborough House that afternoon which will be attended by Her Majesty the Queen Mother.
Invitations to these functions will be sent upon request to three groups: (a) to each surviving holder of the Victoria Cross and one near relative; (b) to two near relatives of each posthumous recipient, one of whom must be the person to whom the medal was actually presented; and (c) to one near relative-parent, brother, sister, widow or child -of each deceased holder of the Victoria Cross.
The government of the United Kingdom has asked us to undertake the task of ascertaining the names and addresses of those eligible persons who would like to receive invitations. The interdepartmental committee to which I referred earlier has been charged with the responsibility of looking after this and other matters connected with the trip. This committee is endeavouring to contact by letter those eligible persons for whom we have addresses, to advise them of the celebrations and to ascertain if they plan to attend.
I would point out, however, that we do not have the addresses of all those who may be


eligible to receive invitations and that some of the addresses we have may not be up to date. To ensure that no one is unaware of this centenary and the invitations which are available, the committee suggests that those who consider themselves eligible write as soon as possible to the deputy minister of the Department of Veterans Affairs. We hope, too, that the veterans organizations in Canada will help us to find those who are eligible and who, otherwise, might be missed.
Finally, in order to assist those who receive Her Majesty's invitations to attend the ceremonies, the government is making arrangements to provide free return transportation from their homes to London. It is expected that they will have approximately one week in England before commencing the return trip.

speechtext:
I
should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In view of the fact that the international wheat agreement conference is to take place in Geneva on the 20th of this month, would the minister say who the representatives from Canada will be; are they being given specific instructions as to the limitations within which the prices shall be supported by them; and, finally, what are the prospects of Britain rejoining the international wheat agreement?

speakeroldname: Righi Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: CANADIAN REPRESENTATIVES AT INTERNATIONAL WHEAT AGREEMENT CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the meeting at Geneva begins in the course of a day or two. Our delegation is headed by the associate deputy minister of the department, Mr. Sharp. However, Mr. Sharp cannot leave for there immediately and will join the delegation later. At the moment it is headed by Mr. McNamara, one of the members of the wheat board. Associated with him is Mr. Charles Wilson, who is one of the officers of the department responsible for wheat matters in Europe. There are also six farm advisers attending, including the heads of the three wheat pools, the head of the United Grain Growers, the head of the Canadian council of agriculture and the head of the Saskatchewan farmers' union. These six delegates are there now.
The instructions are generally that we would like to see the wheat agreement be continued much in the form that it is in today. We are not prepared to take any material reduction in the floor price. There is some flexibility in our views about the maximum

price. We will only be interested if a substantial quantity of wheat is included in the agreement. We think that about two-thirds of the wheat entering into the channels of commerce is the minimum that could be considered. Aside from that, the instructions of the delegation are to negotiate in the hope that a satisfactory agreement can be arranged.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Wednesday, February 15, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe (Port * Arthur) for the second reading of Bill No. 82, to provide for shortterm credit to grain producers in the prairie

Grain
provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Johnson (Kindersley).

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house closed at six o'clock yesterday I was at the point of drawing attention to the fact that the policy, or lack of policy as the case may be, followed by the present government with respect to the grain delivery crisis was in fact undermining the whole system of orderly marketing of grain in Canada.
I had drawn attention to the fact that in 1946 and subsequent years the government of Canada sold the idea to the grain producers of a stabilized system of marketing and that on the basis of their undertaking to market the grain through the Canadian wheat board and under the terms of the British wheat agreement and later through the international wheat agreement the grain producers of Canada were prepared to accept a ceiling price on their grain and in fact did accept a lower price than was offered on the open market at that time on the understanding that this was being done in the interests of stabilized marketing both from the point of view of price and from the point of view of supply.
What has transpired since then has indicated that the government has failed to carry out its share of the bargain, and the present grain delivery crisis with which this house is concerned and which is the reason for this bill which is now before us is only an indication that at the present time the government is attempting to get rid of the responsibility which it had taken on in good faith and which the farmer had accepted in good faith back in 1946.
I believe that this is one of the most important issues in relation to the legislation we are now discussing; that is, unless effective steps are taken by this parliament to assure to the grain producer that he shall receive cash for his grain and that he shall have an opportunity to deliver that grain within a reasonable length of time to the wheat board, then the whole principle underlying the question of orderly marketing will be seriously undermined.
That is one of the reasons why members of the C.C.F. group who have always stood foursquare for the principle of orderly marketing and the principle of the Canadian wheat board have so anxiously been following up this question to place squarely before this house and the country the dangers which may arise out of the lack of action on the part of the government to meet the responsibilities which are inherent in this whole question.
I think that if the government were prepared to give three assurances to the grain producers of Canada it would go a long way towards allaying the fears and anxiety which are very real and which I must assure the government are more real than is sometimes evident from the remarks made in this house across the floor from here. A genuine anxiety exists as to what the future holds for the Canadian grain producers.
If the government could give an assurance to Canadian agriculture that it is willing to accept the principle of parity prices, that in itself would go a long way towards allaying the anxiety under which grain producers of the west and farmers in general are now suffering.
If the government could assure the grain producer at this time that it is prepared to set a floor for export wheat of $1.55 a bushel and that it is willing to provide a floor price for domestic consumption which would be as close to parity as possible-at the present time it is calculated that it would be about $2.20 per bushel-that second assurance would go a long way towards allaying the fears which the grain producers have.
And, as a third assurance, if the government could assure the farmers that it is taking concrete and effective steps to assure that the grain which is now on the farms will be delivered or facilities will be provided for it to be delivered within a reasonable time to the grain elevators, that again would go a long way to allay those anxieties.
But as this debate has progressed to this point none of these assurances have been forthcoming. That is one of the reasons why I believe it would be advisable to place this whole question, the subject matter of this bill which is now before us, the whole question of how to get cash into the hands of the farmers who have produced the grain and are holding it available for delivery, which means that they have fulfilled their part of the contract; what is the best way in which to convert that grain into cash now, next year, the year after and so on. This bill as it now stands does not even begin to deal with that question.
It is a very narrow bill providing for guarantees to the banks. It has many weaknesses and therefore is completely unsatisfactory. I am sure that if this whole question were referred to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization, as is called for by the amendment now before the house, we would have an opportunity to call in representatives of the various farm organizations in Canada, of the three prairie wheat pools and of any other interested organizations, as well as other persons who had

Grain
some advice to offer and who, together with hon. members who are members of that committee, could hammer out an agricultural policy that would mean something, that would have some stability and some future, and not something made up of bits and pieces, of expediency. It would be something based on sound economic principles and sound agricultural principles. It is something which is overdue, it is something which is needed.
I find it most difficult to understand why hon. members who support the government, or members of the government, should take a stand against the acceptance of this amendment. All that the amendment asks for is that the whole question be referred to the standing committee which is constituted for that very purpose. Why do we have a standing committee on agriculture and colonization if it is not to deal with this kind of problem? Why should the government or the members supporting the government take the stand that that committee, which after all has a majority representation from the supporters of the government, which is made up of members from all sides of the house-why should that committee not be trusted to carry out the functions which it was intended to carry out?
I want to make a particular appeal to my colleagues from the province of Manitoba. We have not heard very much in this debate so far from members supporting the government from the province of Manitoba. Apart from the hon. member from Provencher (Mr. Jutras), we have not heard from any other hon. member. Most significant of all, we have not heard from the only minister in the cabinet from the province of Manitoba, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson). I would hope that before this debate is over he would take advantage of this opportunity to tell the house what in his opinion are the wishes and desires of the farmers of the province of Manitoba.
I want to make this appeal to them on this occasion. Let them vote for this amendment on its merits. It has been amply pointed out that there is no need whatever for the government or any supporter of the government to regard this amendment as a motion of want of confidence. The amendment calls for what I would consider to be an efficient and effective method of dealing with a problem which has many implications. We are asking that it be submitted to the proper committee of this house, a committee which incidentally has a member from Manitoba as chairman. Certainly he should be the last one to object to having this question placed before the committee where it belongs.

I appeal to them to approach the members of the government. I do not think it is too late to ask the government to change its mind on this question. It has changed its mind before. I remember not so many months ago when the government said, "Never, never, never" and then at the end said, "Well, hardly ever". The members of the government did change their minds and I think they should change their minds again.
I appeal to my colleagues from Manitoba. For example, does the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Weaver) think that the farmers in the Swan river valley are in agreement with the subject matter of this bill as it now stands, or does he think that perhaps they have something better to offer? I would ask the Minister of Justice if he thinks that the farmers in the area of Minnedosa, for example, are in favour of this bill. If he is in any doubt at all, all he has to do is to refer to the press clippings to refresh his memory.
I would ask the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Weir) if he thinks the farmers of the Portage plain are content with the legislation the government is now proposing and if they have not already expressed themselves rather strongly in favour of a different method, namely the method of cash advances suggested by the C.C.F. I would ask the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Pommer) whether the farmers in his constituency are satisfied with this bill.
I need hardly ask the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Weselak) what the farmers in his constituency think, because along with the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) I had the privilege of attending a meeting at which the hon. member for Springfield was also present which was held in the town of Beausejour in that constituency. It was a most interesting and I think most effective meeting. The farmers who gathered there left no doubt in anyone's mind, including the mind of the hon. member for Springfield, as to where they stood on this question of cash advances as opposed to this bank loan bill.
I ask those hon. members who represent the farmers of Manitoba along with the rest of us whether they feel deep down in their hearts that they are doing the right thing by the people whom they represent, either by keeping silent or by acquiescing or giving approval to this bill, which is simply a cheap substitute for what the farmers are really asking for. If they are not satisfied, and I am sure they are not and they know the people whom they represent are not, then I think it is their duty as members of this

Grain
house, as representatives of western agriculture, not only to say so on the floor of this house but to say so in caucus and directly to the ministers who lead this government.
They should tell them that on this occasion it is the desire of this house, the desire of the membership of this house, that we have a free vote. I ask the government to call off the whips, to remove the shackles of unquestioning approval which they always seek from their supporters, or acquiescence, and on this occasion allow them to express themselves on this amendment both verbally and by their votes, on the basis of what they actually feel is the opinion and desire of the people whom they represent. Let this parliament carry out its function as a democratic parliament, let it not be regarded merely as the tool of a tyrannical ministry.
I think one of the measures of the greatness of any statesman in any government is the ability to change his mind when he feels he has made a mistake. We often hear eulogies of praise for Sir Winston Churchill, one of the outstanding statesmen of the day. Those who have read even his own words about his own life have been struck by the number of times he changed his mind about most serious matters in his own country and in the international sphere. It is perhaps a measure of the greatness of a man who is big enough to admit that under changing circumstances and conditions he is willing to revise his opinion.
I think that that would be a wise move on the part of the government today. Certainly this debate, if it has indicated anything, has indicated that the government has made a comedy of errors right down the line. They started out wrong to begin with. Last fall when this issue became a live one on the prairies-it did not come up overnight- as soon as the new crop year began on August 1, 1955, the farm organizations and members of parliament from the west were already warning the government that there was going to be a serious grain delivery crisis affecting the prairie farmers. The government knew, certainly as early as mid-September, that something would have to be done by this parliament to provide some system under which the farmers could obtain cash in order to convert their surplus grain or grain in storage into cash in order to carry on with their farm operations.
The wise thing to have done, the democratic thing to have done, was to call a special session of parliament in the middle of October or early in November. The members of this house could have devoted their time and their energies to the solution of that
problem in a democratic fashion. The committee on agriculture could have been called together immediately. Representations could have been heard from the various farm organizations across Canada, instead of having to hold a grain conference in Saskatoon. They sent a small delegation to Ottawa to interview the cabinet, and to this day nobody seems to have the full version of what transpired at that meeting. We hear claims and counter claims. We hear that a certain minister of agriculture-for example, our own minister from Manitoba, who left Winnipeg fully instructed by his caucus to ask for cash advances for grain-somehow along the way, by the time he got down to Ottawa, found he was satisfied with bank loans.
All these things have become a mass of confusion through the inactivity of the government and its failure to call a special session of parliament in order to meet the problem at the time it was developing. Now the time has passed, and we are trying to deal with something that should have been dealt with four or five months ago and which could have been much more effectively and intelligently dealt with at that time with the advice of the farm organizations and the wheat pools, which was available to us at that time.
Even now, while the members supporting the government try to convince us that this bill before us is what the farm organizations asked for, we find that the Liberal leaders of the various provincial sections seem to contradict that very statement. Some of you may have been watching television yesterday evening. There was' a program called "Press Conference" in which the leader of the Liberal party of Alberta, Mr. Prowse, appeared. Among the questions before the panel was the question of cash advances versus this present bill. Under close questioning the Liberal leader of that province stated quite categorically that he personally was in favour of cash advances and he was not satisfied with the present bill, although he did try to make a sort of lefthanded justification for it by saying that after all the only farmers who will really bother to apply at all under this legislation are the ones who desperately need it and so it would not involve many people anyway. In other words, he tried to justify it by saying it would not be used much anyway and so it did not matter, but he was careful to place himself on record as being in favour of cash advances. One can understand his caution. Considering what has happened in the past to Liberals who have appeared on television, I think he is to be commended for his caution.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. It just so happens that the views expressed by

the interprovincial farm union were so identical with the ones I hold that I merely referred to that fact. The reasons why, in my opinion, this bill does not do what is required, are several. For example take the banking facilities. It is pointed out that in the province of Saskatchewan there are 1,200 shipping points for grain but only 196 points that are served by banks. In the province of Alberta there are only 159 points with banking facilities, and in Manitoba only 91 points with banking facilities. The whole question of cash advances could have been, and may still be, handled through the wheat board and the elevator agents, which would make it possible for any farmer at any shipping point to go to his elevator agent with his permit book and get his advance. Instead of that they are being asked to seek the services of the banks where facilities are not so widespread and also where there is no guarantee or assurance that any particular farmer will obtain the loan he seeks.
One of the great disabilities is the fact that not only is there a form to be filled out in order to establish the farmer's credit but also there are deductions to be made from the grain he has already delivered. As 1 believe the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) pointed out the other day, in many cases farmers with sufficient grain on their farms to warrant a good credit standing, but who may have been fortunate enough to deliver some of their quota before this date, find they are not able under this legislation to borrow one cent because of the deductions that have to be made first from the grain they have already delivered before they can apply for a further loan.
Then there is the whole question-and perhaps it is a very important consideration- of the experiences that farmers have had with banks and with loan and mortgage companies in the past. I hope they have not all been unhappy experiences, but unfortunately we know that in the prairies many of the experiences in the past have been very unhappy. Farmers have borrowed in good faith, in times when the grain was worth something, a relatively small amount of money, $600 or $800. Then the grain prices fell seriously, and they had to pay back the dollars they had borrowed with production that had to be doubled in volume to provide for the same dollars. The farmer who borrowed at one time $800 found he had paid back $1,200 and, owing to the compound interest, arrears and so on, he still owed $800.
All these experiences have not been forgotten and the farmers are wondering why it is that the government insists that those who can obtain loans be forced to go again

Grain
to the banks and have to pay 5 per cent interest when as a matter of fact the government has a moral responsibility, if not a legal one, to accept grain deliveries, provide facilities for those grain deliveries and provide the farmers with the cash they have already earned. I therefore hope that the private members who sit opposite us and support the government will on this occasion assert their responsibility and authority in the house by speaking to the ministers of the cabinet and asking them to declare a free vote. Let us have a free expression of opinion. If that is done I think there is no doubt that hon. members will find it wise to accept the amendment referring this matter to the committee that has been established to consider such questions so that it may find a lasting solution to this important problem.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of dealing with certain questions that have arisen during the last few days, to reiterate my opposition to the bill now before the house, and to give reasons why the amendment should be supported. I go back to the legislation of 1951. I have heard about this act on many occasions. The minister has mentioned more than once in the house that the act of 1951 entitled "The Prairie Grain Producers' Interim Financing Act" was unsuccessful and achieved very little in providing credit for western farmers. One of the major reasons for that failure was the fact that it was studded with iniquitous provisions for enforcement. One of those iniquitous provisions in the act of 1951 was this:
9. (1) A person who
(a)	states in his application an estimated quantity of crops or grain or an estimated amount that he knows to be false; or
(b)	makes any other statement in his application that is false in any material respect;
is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction to a fine of not less than twenty-five dollars and not more than five hundred dollars.
In addition, under subsection 2 upon conviction he shall be ordered to pay a penalty equal to the amount of any guaranteed loan made by him in respect of which the offence was committed as has not been repaid by him, with interest thereon to the date of the conviction. That was the first occasion in my experience that imprisonment for debt was made part of the laws of this country since imprisonment for debt was abolished many, many years ago. That section in its original form is intensified in the new bill. It is unjust and unfair. Indeed, Shylock himself could learn how to extract a pound of flesh by simply reading the sections dealing with penalties in the present bill which make every farmer who makes a mistake in the forms he has to complete liable not only to
a fine and, in default, imprisonment, but in addition a penalty to the extent of the amount of his loan. Why that was continued in the present legislation is beyond me.
That is one of the reasons why the 1951 act did not operate. When this party took the stand the other day on the resolution stage that it would support the introduction of the measure with a view to ascertaining what, the bill was, nobody here or anywhere else had any belief that the government would include such provisions in the bill as have been included.
I am going back a way to deal with the circuitous course taken by the government and in particular by the minister himself in connection with the matter. First of all, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said that the farmers did not really need money, and I think the Prime Minister is still the head of the government although there are others who doubt it. According to him, no money was needed. The farmers are not asking for much. Ridicule was heaped upon those who attended meetings in western Canada. Only today a representation was made by the interprovincial farm union council of the western provinces which indicates the almost universal demand for cash advances on farm-stored wheat everywhere throughout the west. I read from that representation, for it represents the facts:
Scores of mass protest meetings, resolutions and petitions that have developed spontaneously throughout the west accurately indicate the degree of dissatisfaction felt in rural areas regarding the guaranteed bank loans on farm-stored grain. It is felt almost unanimously that farmers should not be asked to burden themselves with added debt and interest charges because wheat is not being sold at a sufficient volume to enable the farmer to maintain his cash position.
Then they go on to point out the weaknesses of this procedure. As was indicated in his concluding remarks by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, it all results from the failure to call parliament together. It is the old, old game. When in doubt pass an order in council. Sometimes do not even bother to pass an order in council, just believe you did and proceed to act accordingly. You find out afterwards that you did not even go to that trouble because, after all, if you can legislate by order in council behind closed doors it is so much easier to save the trouble of passing an order in council. I continue with the representations of the farm union council:
Banking facilities are not readily available in many parts of the prairie provinces.
I am not going to follow that any further because that point has been dealt with.
The amount of red tape involved in securing acceptance of a bank loan application is so great

Grain
as to discourage all but the most persistent, and eliminates a good percentage of those who might otherwise qualify.
It were easier, Mr. Speaker, for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for anyone to pass the catechism and examination that is required in order to secure a loan. I repeat what I said the other day. The banks are turning down applications as soon as they find out the uses that are to be made of the money in the event they decide that the use is one that does not come within the ambit of the legislation.
The first excuse given by the government was that the farmers did not need money, that all was well. When that subterfuge and distortion of the facts was unsuccessful the right hon. gentleman produced the next story. He said that what these people who support cash advances are trying to do, indirectly or possibly directly, is to destroy the wheat board. There was a bogey! They really had one there. I am going to read the minister's words as found at page 127 of Hansard of January 16. He said:
The chairman of the board has been in the service of the government for 25 years, his duties associated solely with the marketing of western grain. Associated with him are three very able men who share in the work of the board. I can tell the house that, if the government instructed the wheat board to lend money on farm-stored grain and assume the responsibility for the lending of that money and its subsequent collection, the four members of the wheat board would be out of office within a matter of days.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Order. Did I understand that the hon. member was reading from page 127? He will realize that is a different debate of the same session.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker. I should have summarized it. To summarize the minister's words, he said: "I can tell you that if this happened the wheat board would be out." Of all the unmitigated nonsense that the minister has brought forth, that indeed wins prize No. 1. I tried to find out what had been done in this connection and the only way I could find out was simply by asking a question to ascertain what the situation was. As appears at page 992 of Hansard I asked these questions:
1.	Did the chairman or any members of the wheat board notify the government at any time since July 1, 1955, that they would resign within a matter of days if loans on farm-stored wheat were brought into effect? If so, which of them did so?
2.	What was the date or dates of said notification and were same given verbally or in writing?
Answer by Mr. Howe (Port Arthur):
1.	No.
2.	Answered by No. 1 above.
I saw immediately that there was a loophole there because I referred to loans. So

I redrafted the question in order to get the truth. Then to my surprise the Department of Trade and Commerce gave the same answer as reported at page 1096 of Hansard. The question was:
1. Did the chairman or any members of the wheat board notify the government at any time since July 1, 1955, that they would resign within a matter of days if cash advances on farm-stored wheat were brought into effect?
The answer given was no.
Mr. Speaker, that was just another of those self-created subterfuges by the right hon. gentleman to evade the demands of western farmers to have action in this regard. Grain

The board shall, if directed by regulation, pay to each producer at the time of delivery of wheat to the board, in addition to any other payment authorized by this section, a sum per bushel on account of storage of the said wheat on the producer's farm, for such period of storage as the board in its sole discretion shall fix for the purposes of such storage payment, which sum, however, shall equal the amount payable for storage in a country elevator for the same period . . .

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take a few brief moments simply to underline and endorse the themes which my farmer colleagues have been presenting, and

when I say "farmer colleagues" I mean just that, because we are fortunate that in discussing this particular question we have in our group some young and active farmers. The house may judge for itself whether or not they have proved that activity in this particular debate.
There is one respect in which we are fortunate in this debate and in which we are not always so fortunate, and that is that we have been able to get directives from our constituents. I do not suggest that we always take directives from our constituents but we certainly consider what they have to say and this is one debate in which we have had ample opportunity to assess the opinion of various sections of the community in regard to the particular piece of legislation which has been amended by the motion that we have moved.
The things I do want to say today, and I say it with all sincerity and earnestness, is that the bill does not reflect in either its letter or spirit the decision of the Saskatoon conference, discussion of which has occupied some time in this present debate.
You know, farmers in western Canada are blamed for many things. One example of this was advanced to me in a letter from a farmer in eastern Canada. He said the farmers in the west have already received too much consideration; they talk about $65 million. Well, we dealt with that the other day. Our eastern friends are liable to forget that that $65 million was given in lieu of moneys which the farmers would have received under other circumstances during the period of the war.
Another reason I was asked to support this bill, and this is a peculiar reason, is that some eastern farmers say that the western farmers send down to them rubbish feed with which to feed their livestock. I shall take just one moment to answer that particular item because it is important to the people in the maritimes and the mid-Canada provinces.
As far as this question of feed is concerned, when the farmer delivers his wheat to the elevator the screenings pass out of his ownership into the hands of the elevator company. If my hon. friends in eastern Canada want pure feed grain, and I do not see why they should not have it, then I suggest that they buy directly from the wheat board or from the grain companies. They can buy No. 3 barley or No. 1 feed oats or whatever it is they want on the Winnipeg market, under government certificate, have it brought down to eastern Canada, build their own storage on a cooperative basis or some other method, grind the grain and distribute it among their

Grain
members. Then they would not be depending upon the grain dealers who are presently selling them a mixture of wild oats, pigweed and buckwheat, as I have seen being fed to pigs in Prince Edward Island. However, I imagine I will be out of order if I pursue that any further.
Coming back to this main question, I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in all sincerity that I think he made a tremendous mistake when he attributed to us, and I am sure equally to other members in this house, a political motive in opposing this legislation. After all, everything we do in this house is political. I understand politics to be the science of government. If any political praise is due because of what we have done, that is fine.
I say in all sincerity that I think the minister is vastly mistaken. As I said when I opened my remarks, we have had time to make contacts in a way the minister has not. We have been able to get the real opinion of the people of the country in regard to this measure. I know I can only interpret what the minister was thinking, but my interpretation is that he felt that in our hearts we realized that this bill was better than nothing, that we were simply opposing it for political purposes and at the last moment would throw up the sponge and say, "Yes, we will vote for it because it is better than nothing."
We do not think it is better than nothing. We do not say that it is vicious legislation, but we say it is silly and useless legislation. It is taking the place of legislation which would better meet the wishes of those who are so greatly concerned. Somebody said the other day that we should not indulge in humour when dealing with a matter as serious as this, but I say in all sincerity to the minister and the government that in western Canada this legislation is considered as a joke.
There are many retired farmers in my constituency but there are also active farmers there because my constituency runs south of the city. Saskatoon is the headquarters of the Saskatchewan farmers' union and we are in contact with farming people. Our very life depends on the success of the farmers who are contiguous to the city. We are the distributing point for goods and services to meet the needs of farmers all over northern Saskatchewan. I have not met one farmer who actually said to me that he thought this legislation was good, and I have not met anyone who said that he thought this legislation was better than nothing.
We have a good deal of labour in our city and I am glad to say that the labour unions are expressing a good deal of sympathy for
their fellow men in the farm union. Several of the labour organizations got together and passed a resolution attacking this particular legislation as it was forecast on the radio and in the press before it was brought in. They realized that their prosperity depends upon the prosperity of the farmers.
What about the political parties? The Liberal party in Saskatchewan has done a pretty good job of covering up. We have had an example of that in the house here in the various speeches by the hon. member for Kosthern (Mr. Tucker) who has tried to make out that in fact this is what the farmers have asked for. But the Liberal association in Saskatoon does not think that this is what they want. I have the record in my hand but the previous Speaker said that we are not allowed to read these things and therefore I shall not attempt to do that. That Liberal association in meeting was severely critical of the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce and furthermore they said that if they were supporting a bank loan, and being a Liberal association they said they would support a bank loan, they criticized the rate of interest as being much too high.
Speaking of politics, a Liberal convention at Souris-Estevan met together to nominate a Liberal candidate. What did they do? They nominated the sitting Conservative member who said to them, and I am quoting his words, "I am a Conservative." However, they let it go at that. So much for what people think about this particular legislation.
I want to come back to this question of what really did go on at the Saskatoon conference as I think that is the crux of the argument put forward by the hon. member for Rosthern. I should like to quote what the hon. member said, as reported on page 1159 of Hansard of February 14. The hon. member was speaking in this particular debate and he said:
I told this house, and it was objected to over and over again by the C.C.F. opposite, that this marketing conference had unanimously endorsed the idea of cash advances, but it left open the whole question of the mechanics by which those advances should be made.
That was the Saskatoon conference the hon. member was talking about.
Hon. members will recall how that suggestion was jeered at by members of the C.C.F. opposition.
No wonder. I sat at that conference for three days and I know what went on. The hon. member then made this statement:
I have now brought this submission, signed on behalf of the government of Saskatchewan, endorsing every word I said.
Anyone reading that would take it as a reference to a submission by the Saskatoon

Grain
conference, but it was no such thing. That was a request submitted by a delegation from that Saskatoon conference which came down here to present their recommendations to the government. That delegation was composed of representatives of the U.G.G.-I believe the president was a member-as well as other grain companies. There were lots of people there representing people other than farmers, as well as farmers. There were people of all political opinions. When they got together they presented to the government the only thing on which they were unanimous, and that was that there should be cash advances paid on wheat stored on the farm. Now, it is very interesting. There is a difference whether you are talking about the Saskatoon conference or whether you are talking about the request made to the government by a number of delegates of various political colours and various occupations who happened-

speechtext:
I shall answer by saying this. Never have I seen farmers so angry-and I count among those farmers Mr. Nollet, the minister of agriculture of the province of Saskatchewan, whose language in that regard [ dare not quote in this house-at their disappointment and disgust with this wishy-washy thing, as they call it, that had been presented to the Canadian government. The only reason it was wishy-washy was that it was the only thing on which they could get those people with various types of interests unanimous. As far as the farmers were concerned, they considered they had been bypassed. Most of them used the word "sabotaged".
I want to deal for one moment with the assertion of the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) that what this government is doing in this legislation is in fact what was requested by the Saskatoon conference. I am not going to read this but I am just going to say that after the reports of what happened at the Saskatoon conference this was stated in a reliable newspaper:
It was also stressed that this was an advance and not a loan.
That is from a report of the Saskatoon conference. It is rather an amazing thing that, when the hon. member for Rosthern

himself wrote a letter to the Winnipeg Free Press shortly after this incident, the hon. member said:
At the Saskatoon conference, farm union leaders and others advocated that advances should be made to farmers against wheat in store on their farms by the wheat board through the elevator agents.
Those are not my words, but the words of my hon. friend from Rosthern. Let him eat them now. I think that should settle the question of the Saskatoon conference, and of the representations that were made here. But I can assure the government and the minister that, so far as all these people are concerned -the people with whom I had daily contact for two or three weeks in my own city and outside it-whether they be professional men, labour men or farmers or whatever they may be, they consider the government legislation in this case as nothing short of a joke. That is absolutely true. I have already dealt with my hon. friend from Rosthern. If he talks, as I said the other day, till he is blue in the face -and he gets that way occasionally,-of course we have to make allowances for my hon. friend because he does not like the C.C.F. party and he has good reason for that. After all, he is smarting under the rather unfortunate and unsuccessful experiences he has had with the C.C.F. in the province of Saskatchewan over the past five or six years.
I do not think there is anything more I can say in that regard, because I believe I have made my point; but there is also one other point. That is the assertion that the Saskatchewan government somehow subscribes to this silly business of a loan because the minister of agriculture from the province of Saskatchewan signed his name to this wishy-washy document that was produced and presented to the cabinet here in Ottawa. Mr. Speaker, your predecessor has precluded our reading these documents in the house, although I notice you have been a little more lenient, and I shall not attempt to do so. But I could read here speech after speech made by the premier of the province of Saskatchewan, who, whatever he may be, to my thinking is a great man and certainly represents the C.C.F. opinion in that province of Saskatchewan. In everything he has said he has been against this principle of bank loans and has been in favour-and in fact he has laid it down on the line that this should be done-of cash advances, a payment in advance without interest on grain stored on the farm.
Needless to say, I shall support this amendment. We could have had something better, but under the circumstances I think we can support that. Early in this debate

Grain
we were challenged. We had the most amazing spectacle of the Minister of Trade and Commerce getting up one night in a fury- and that is the only way I can describe it-, looking at our friend from Regina City (Mr. Ellis) and saying, "All right, if you oppose this, we shall withdraw it." I ask, is this the way for a responsible minister of the crown to act in a democratic House of Commons? A member of a small group in this House of Commons is allowed to twist and change and pervert and cancel of his own volition legislation brought in by a government that is supposed to be acting for the good of the people concerned and for the good of the Canadian nation. Somebody has said we have witnessed a comedy of errors. I am not going into that, but one would need the fingers of both hands to count the errors the government has made in the last two weeks about this and other matters.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
This afternoon I listened to the parliamentary assistant endeavouring as best he could to read into certain resolutions from farm organizations the idea that farm organizations were not in favour of cash advances. He stated that, when the C.C.F. said that farm organizations and the farmers were almost unanimously in favour of cash advances and opposed to bank loans, we were not stating a fact.
I did not have the privilege of attending the Saskatoon conference, but it seems to me clear from the record that the delegates at that convention were in favour of cash advances. It seems also true that when the representatives from that conference met the cabinet they did not make precisely the same presentation to the cabinet that was agreed upon at that conference. Certainly there was a difference of opinion.
The important point is the fact that when the farm leaders, whoever they might have been, who met the cabinet and seemed to support the idea of bank loans, went back to their member bodies and faced their delegates in convention, the delegates speaking on behalf of the producers rejected any suggestion that bank loans were acceptable and those delegates came out spontaneously in favour of cash advances. Almost the same thing that happened in the prairies last fall can be seen in this debate. When the resolution preceding this bill first came before the House of Commons, the C.C.F. members said they were opposed to the resolution. We said we were going to vote against it and against the bill that would . follow the resolution. It is not too easy sometimes to stand alone. It is much easier to be
with the crowd. When you are in the opposition-and there are three opposition parties- it is much easier to go along with the majority. But we said we were against bank loans on principle. We said that, whilst they might do some negligible amount of good in a very few instances, the point was that we were discussing an important principle.
We had already made our stand clear that we were in favour of cash advances when we moved an amendment in the throne speech debate. We made it clear that we were not going to advocate cash advances one day and then be caught standing up in the house and voting for bank loans at a later date; that it was a question of principle; that we were not going to try to ride both horses; that even though we might be misquoted, even though our stand might be twisted, we were going to stand by the principle of cash advances, and the only way we could stand by that principle was to vote against the bank loan legislation all the way down the line.
I think the stand we have taken has already been justified and is now proven to be right. When we see the other opposition parties, both of them, I believe, now prepared to vote against this repugnant bill-

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
We have seen the bill
now.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
You have seen the bill now. The bill is precisely the same measure that the Minister of Trade and Commerce outlined to the Canadian people on his radio and television show, a $1,500 maximum, 5 per cent interest, on surrender of the wheat board permit book and after which 50 per cent of the moneys received from all deliveries will be paid to the bank. I want to congratulate the Social Credit and Conservative groups in the house for being prepared now to change their position when they see that bank loans should be opposed.
As I said, the same thing happened in the west last fall. A conference was held and there were some differences of opinion as to how cash advances might best be made. The leaders came to Ottawa, and apparently there was a greater difference of opinion when they faced the cabinet. Members of this group, other members from other parties and farm leaders went across western Canada speaking to farm organizations and meetings of farmers, and because of that campaign opinion became crystallized in favour of cash advances and opposed to bank loans. As a matter of fact almost all the organizations, as well as the majority of political parties, are now opposed to bank loans and in favour of cash advances. As the days go by, fewer and fewer people are in favour of bank loans.

Grain
The Minister of Trade and Commerce said at one time during this session that he had received about 3,000 pieces of paper with regard to the question of bank loans or cash advances, and I am positive in my own mind that 98 per cent of all the representations that have been made to the Minister of Trade and Commerce have been in favour of cash advances and opposed to bank loans. I would very much like to see that record produced immediately so we can see whether that statement is in fact correct.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am not objecting to what has been placed in the return but I am saying that in my opinion 98 per cent of all the pieces of paper to which the Minister of Trade and Commerce has referred are in favour of cash advances and opposed to bank loans. Nothing that the Minister of Trade and Commerce can say can change the fact that western Canada believes the legislation now before the house is repugnant and should be withdrawn because it is not in the best interests of the agricultural producers.
I do not imagine the Liberal party is unanimously in favour of this legislation. Oh, they may vote unanimously in the house. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has said: "Toe the party line; we are not going to have anyone exercising a free vote, a free opinion." He has even told the hon. gentlemen in the other place who belong to his political party that they too must toe the line.
In Saskatchewan the Minister of Agriculture has already carried out these orders from the Minister of Trade and Commerce and, while there was a lot of deviation in the party line in Saskatchewan last fall, it is now being strictly followed. Nevertheless it is still not true that the Liberal party is unanimously in favour of bank loans. I too saw Mr. Harper Prowse, the Alberta Liberal leader, on television last night in the program "Press Conference". I have never seen the gentleman in person but I want to say that I was rather impressed generally with the ability he showed. It seemed to me that whenever he was being questioned about provincial matters he was very much at home and had the answers. He sat right on top of the conference until somebody mentioned federal policy and asked him about the government's wheat policy. Then he faltered and hesitated. He looked down and picked up a little note.
I can almost see the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) doing about the same

thing on a television show. Then Mr. Prowse read the record, the old record about quantities of grain delivered and produced in the last five years. Then he was asked point blank, "Are you in favour of cash advances?" His answer was "yes"; he was in favour of cash advances.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: He will be liquidated.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I suggest that Harper Prowse represents the opinion of prairie farmers in Alberta when he says that he is in favour of cash advances far more than the Minister of Trade and Commerce represents the opinion of the farmers of Alberta and western Canada generally when he says that the farm organizations are willing to go along with this legislation.
The parliamentary assistant quoted the submission of the federation of agriculture to the cabinet. That submission did not oppose cash advances. I did not hear him read anything about cash advances. But had the parliamentary assistant wished to quote the most important farm organization as far as the production of wheat is concerned, an organization that is a member of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, he would know where the agricultural producers in fact stand on this question.
I am glad that democracy works in parliament to some extent, in spite of statements from members of the cabinet. I am glad to see democracy working in Canada and working in the farm organizations. I believe that the fundamental power must rest with the rank and file. It must be with the membership, with the ordinary citizens. It is a fact that some leaders of some farm organizations were prepared to go along with the bank loan legislation-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: They asked for it, too.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Some of them requested it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
-and the delegates said, "We are opposed to the bank loan legislation; we want cash advances." Democracy exerted itself in these farm organizations and the opinions of some leaders were reversed, but democracy apparently cannot exert itself within the Liberal party or their position would be reversed in the face of the opinion in western Canada. We have seen the Minister of Trade and Commerce in action before. He gets an idea in his head and he says, "This is it." No matter what opinion may be against it, no matter if he stands alone, he is going to see the legislation rammed through the house against all opposition and against . the country itself.

Grain
What did the three pool conventions do? I do not have their resolutions in my hand, but I do have the submission of the interprovincial farm union council presented to the government this day, and it contains a reference to the stand of the three western wheat pools. With regard to cash advances it has this to say:
Therefore the interprovincial farm union council is continuing to press for adoption of its original proposal, which has been endorsed-
I want to emphasize this.
-at the three wheat pool delegate meetings, that the government arrange for interest free cash advances by the Canadian wheat board on farm-stored grain to the value of 50 per cent of the initial payment on an estimated delivery of 8 bushels per cultivated acre.
Nothing could be clearer than the fact that the western farmers want cash advances and are opposed to the legislation that is now before the house. Some reasons have been advanced by the minister as to why cash advances could not be made. None of them have appealed to me. I think all of them are incorrect. I think all of them are unfounded. Whenever the minister stated something by way of reasons why it could not be done those statements cannot be borne out by the facts. I think the minister gave one extremely important reason why he is not prepared to provide cash advances. He had this to say as reported at page 603 of Hansard:
Finally, the government was reluctant to put elevator agents into competition in making wheat board advances.
The government was reluctant to let elevator agents compete for the business of cash advances. That statement is extremely important, because it has a great bearing on the business that would be received by each elevator company at any given marketing point. It has an important bearing on the whole question of box car distribution.
If the government had provided cash advances through the elevator system, a producer at a given marketing point would go to the elevator company where he wished to deliver his grain and obtain from that elevator company the cash advance. Then the farmer would be required to pledge his grain on delivery to that elevator company. Therefore if 50 per cent of the farmers at one marketing point had pledged their grain to a certain elevator company, that elevator company would have to be given 50 per cent of the box cars in order to move the grain so that the farmers who had accepted cash advances could repay them.
If that had been done, the farmers then would have had restored to them the right to deliver grain to the elevator of their choice. It would be the farmer who would decide,
and not the transport controller or the Minister of Trade and Commerce who is deciding to which elevator farmers must deliver the grain because of the lack of box cars and because of the bad distribution of box cars.
If you brought in a system of cash advances, you would be stepping on the toes of some of the private grain interests which we have seen the Minister of Trade and Commerce so anxious to protect over the years. We have seen many times the attitude of the Minister of Trade and Commerce toward the farm organizations. The western farm organizations have asked for a better distribution of box cars. He gave them a transport controller who is doing nothing about the matter, who is opposed to the farm organizations, and who is opposed to allowing the farmers to deliver grain to the elevator of their choice. The statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the government was reluctant to put elevator agents into competition in making wheat board advances is, in my opinion, highly significant. I should like to see a little bit of competition in the grain business, but the minister is opposed to competition. He wants the situation to continue where farmers are forced to deliver grain to whatever elevator may happen to get the box cars.
In this debate the Minister of Trade and Commerce has made a great many statements. The vast majority of the statements and the assertions he has made, I submit, are wrong, incorrect, ill-founded and cannot in any way be supported. The C.C.F. are asking for cash advances. He said, "Oh, yes, you are asking for cash advances. Why? Because you want to embarrass the wheat board. Anybody that is for cash advances is an enemy of the wheat board." He said the farmers' union is something like the C.C.F.; that they have said they support the wheat board "but", and he says there is always an extremely important "but".
The record of the C.C.F. group in regard to the wheat board is clear. We are not obliged to protect our record. We believe in the wheat board system of marketing all grains. That record is clear. I suggest that the farmers' union record is just as clear. They are not here to defend themselves, but their record is just as clear that they are 100 per cent in support of the wheat board system of marketing grain. Therefore the minister's statement to the effect that anybody supporting cash advances is the enemy of the wheat board is in fact wrong and is, in fact, perfectly ridiculous.
The organization that has campaigned most for the Canadian wheat board and in support of orderly marketing is no doubt the Saskatchewan wheat pool. Their delegates in

Grain
convention assembled the first day passed an emergency resolution that reads as follows:
That we urge the government of Canada to make immediate provision for advances to farmers on farm-stored grain.
That advances to farmers on farm-stored grain should be up to one-half the normal delivery expected and repayable on the basis of one-half of the value of each delivery made by the farmer.
That advances on farm-stored grain should be made by way of government-guaranteed loans to the Canadian wheat board; the Canadian wheat board to arrange with elevator companies to make the advances to individual farmers, and that any interest involved in such loans should be absorbed by the federal treasury.
The policy of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, as approved by its delegates in annual meeting, is clear-cut. It does not favour the government's proposal for bank loans. It firmly believes that the conditions are such that extraordinary measures are called for, and that these should include advances against farm-stored grain, and that such advances should be made to individual farmers through elevator companies in accordance with an agreement between the companies and the wheat board.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce says about 100,000 farmer members of the Saskatchewan wheat pool are the enemies of the Canadian wheat board. That is an extremely irresponsible statement from the minister in charge of grain marketing. The minister is always willing to slam anybody. He makes wild statements. Last year when we were discussing another bill in connection with the Canada Grain Act he referred to the wheat pools as the C.C.F. pools. I suppose in the mind of the minister that was calling them just about as bad a name as he could lay his tongue to. So he brushed aside the Saskatchewan wheat pool and the other wheat pools as being C.C.F. pools.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It probably was not a compliment.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Then another statement the Minister of Trade and Commerce has made, which is just as ridiculous and cannot be substantiated, is the one to the effect that the government could not make cash advances because they could not get ample security if it were done through the wheat board, and there was nothing to stop a farmer from feeding his grain to his livestock after he had received a cash advance, or selling his grain to his neighbour.
What was the minister saying? He was saying that the small farmer he had been talking about-the farmer who is poor; the farmer who has some grain but needs some money-could not be trusted if it were done through the wheat board because he might feed the grain some dark night, or he might haul it across to his neighbour.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Big brother is watching him.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
There would be no danger of any farmer getting away with anything under the bank loan legislation. The only way in which he can get out of paying that, I guess, is to drop dead, because he is going to be tied very tightly. But surely the Minister of Trade and Commerce does not believe that any percentage of the farmers at all are not honest or that they would in fact feed or sell grain that was pledged to the elevator system. It is such a ridiculous statement. The farmer would be receiving only half the value of the grain. The wheat board has control of his permit book. In order to obtain the other 50 per cent of the value he must deliver the grain to an elevator. That is another statement by the minister that is completely inaccurate and cannot be substantiated in any way.
After saying that the farmers were not to be trusted, he said, after all, there was not too much need for any legislation. He said he was at a meeting of farm representatives. After the meeting was over one of the farm representatives asked him if he would like a lift in his car. He said the farmer had a new car and remarked to the minister that his land was now clear. The farmer told the minister he had one year's crop in his bins, something for which he had been hoping for many years.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

The minister went on to say that the farmer had a new car, had his farm clear and he had one year's crop in his bins-

speechtext:
the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine

is asking me to rule that the telling of the same story twice in this house is repetition to the extent that repetition is barred by the rules of this house, I am very much afraid I would have to admit that at this time it would be most unfair for me to so rule against the hon. member for Assiniboia, considering other speeches we have heard in this and other debates.
At the same time, I feel that the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine is giving voice to views which are held by a great many in this house, and with which I believe the hon. member who now has the floor will agree, that little can be added to a debate by repetition of what has been said before. When repetition reaches a certain stage it becomes an abuse of the privilege of this house. All hon. members on all sides I think will agree that that situation can arise. Perhaps I might express a personal opinion that we are close to it, but I am not going to rule at the moment that the hon. member has gone that far.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
In one breath, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Trade and Commerce says this legislation is necessary to help the small farmer, the farmer who is short of money. He says we cannot establish a system of cash advances because the farmers cannot be trusted. Then he changes his story and says that after all, the farmers of western Canada are still well off. They are driving new cars. They have their land clear. I think the fact is that only a tiny percentage of western farmers are driving new cars. The vast majority are driving cars that are now a few years old. They are almost all heavily in debt. They are short of money. They are honest and they want cash advances. I believe they will resent the statement of the minister that they are all well off and there is nothing for them to worry about.
The minister made another statement to which I believe reference was made this afternoon, although I was not in the chamber at the time, by the hon. member for Prince Albert. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said that if a system of cash advances were put through parliament he would be faced with the resignation of the members of the Canadian wheat board. I may tell you that jolted me. I could scarcely believe my ears. I know the members of the Canadian wheat board and I have every respect for them as individuals. Personally, I believe that if parliament asked the wheat board to provide a system of cash advances, the present members of the Canadian wheat board would be only too pleased to carry out the will of parliament.
Grain
I can recall an earlier statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, when he said we could not have a new system of box car distribution based on farmers shipping to the elevator of their choice because if we did the transport controller would resign. He would fold up. There would be no transport controller. Last year before the agriculture committee the transport controller was beginning to say very much the same thing; he could not administer it. I asked him point blank, "If parliament passed legislation directing you to control box cars in a certain way, would you implement the law as passed by parliament?" The transport controller said, yes; he would not resign but would be right on the job attempting to enforce the law of the country.
The minister said the wheat board would resign. Then the hon. member for Prince Albert asked a number of questions as to the date the minister received that information as to their impending resignation if cash advances were provided. The answer was no. Here we have more bluff, more inaccurate statements, more excuses and more threats. The minister has got himself in a jam. He is up to his ears in trouble, and it is all his own fault because he refuses to stick to the facts. He keeps on making statements that are ridiculous. He looks foolish in the house and in the country. He is not undermining the Canadian wheat board or the orderly marketing system by making these statements, but he is undermining the Liberal party in western Canada. He is undermining his own prestige in western Canada. A few years ago he had a lot of prestige. A few years ago in the books of Canadian farm organizations his name was respected, but today his name is not respected.
The Minister of Agriculture can shade meanings. He can pop down a hole any time you believe you are catching him. He will even go to Hansard and do something with the record, put something in or take something out. The Minister of Agriculture is well known in western Canada. But the Minister of Trade and Commerce does not follow the example set by the Minister of Agriculture. He makes statements right on the record that cannot be substantiated in any way and which time after time are proven inaccurate. He does not care about the record. So in western Canada, although the reputation of the Minister of Agriculture was not particularly high, now in comparison with that of the Minister of Trade and Commerce he probably stands in a higher position, even though the reputation of the Minister of Agriculture leaves a great deal to be desired.

Grain
The Minister of Trade and Commerce did not end the statements he could not substantiate with the one to which I have just referred. He keeps on making them, and is not at all discouraged if he is proven wrong every time he makes a speech. Speaking on the system in the United States for cash advances or loans, he had this to say:
It has been said frequently here that in the United States grain in the farmer's bin is paid for by the government, but that is not true.
That can be found at page 1032 of Hansard. The minister says it is not true that grain in farmers' bins in the United States can be paid for. I hold in my hand a copy of Price Programs, a publication of the United States department of agriculture and I quote from page 17:
Q. What kind of farm storage must a producer have to be eligible for CCC loans-

The minister then goes on to say at page 1032 of Hansard:
We, in Canada, cannot have anything to do with the grain until it is delivered into the government's licensed storage. The two are practically the same.
In answering that statement I will deal with the comments of the parliamentary assistant that the United States proposal is loans. That is what they call them; they are loans. I will tell you what kind of loan it is and if the farmers of western Canada could have this type of loan I am sure they would be 100 per cent in favour of it.
The farmer in the United States today can get from the CCC a loan of $2.08 a bushel for the wheat in his bin; that is the national farm average. What is the interest? Three and one-half per cent. When does the farmer pay the interest? He pays it only when he wishes to discharge the loan by paying it in cash. But when he delivers his grain to the CCC the interest is cancelled. The interest is cancelled when the grain is

delivered to the Commodity Credit Corporation. Therefore the United States farmer can get something worth while. The Minister of Trade and Commerce says the systems are just the same, but the Canadian farmer can get nothing except a bank loan and only then if the banker is in a good humour and likes the look of the farmer when he comes in to make his application.
The United States farmer can get $2.08 a bushel on his grain without interest immediately after it is harvested, because the interest is cancelled whenever the CCC takes the grain from the farmer the following spring.

The strength of this lien is 100 per cent, and nothing can supersede it. The strength does not flow from the Bank Act but flows from this legislation which is now before parliament.
