Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I do so with certain qualms of conscience because it is going to be very difficult to say anything that has not already been said by someone else. However, I do think we could say a lot yet on the merits or the demerits of the bill which is before the house at the present time.
I think if we were to be a little more realistic in our thinking we should go back a little further than this and deal with the
root cause and the necessity of presenting a bill such as this. I think if we were to be realistic in our thinking we would have to agree that there is a challenge here to the people who are responsible for the fiscal policies of this government.
I think it even goes beyond that. I think it is really a condemnation of our fiscal policy. In this bill I believe we are just trying to determine whether or not it is better to give an aspirin or a dose of alka seltzer to relieve our economic headache. I do not think we are getting to the root of this problem. If mother nature is kind next year and we have another bumper crop, we will have to come back and repeat that order.
I do not think anyone should assume that he is ruling by divine right. Members of parliament are elected as individuals, they are not collectively grouped and elected as a government at all. Naturally those who are in the majority are charged with the responsibility of administering the business of this country, but that does not give them any right, in my opinion, to assume that they are there by divine right. They should not take us back to the law of the jungle and assume that might is right. They should be prepared to listen to constructive criticism by the people who are so vitally concerned with agriculture.
We have had the results of the collective thinking and good judgment of the important people in Alberta, Manitoba and Saskatchewan; of the farm organizations which have been charged with the responsibility at the local level. They have tried to come up with the right answers and suggestions in order to help those who in the final analysis are charged with the responsibility of doing something about this problem.
This government would be well advised to listen to the suggestions that have been made, the suggestions that the best way to serve the interests of the farmer is not by allowing him to borrow another $1,500 of his own money at 5 per cent but rather to give him advances of up to 50 per cent for grain stored on the farm. If we took a more realistic attitude and concentrated upon trying to determine ways and means of selling our wheat I think we would be getting closer to our responsibility.
I do not think we grow wheat or anything else just for the sake of putting it in a granary, storing it and getting money on it, either through the medium of bank loans or advances. Until we get down to basic facts and apply to our fiscal policy some modern techniques of salesmanship we will have this to contend with year after year. You can scarcely listen to a radio program or watch

Grain
a television show without having demonstrated to you new techniques in salesmanship. That is done as a matter of necessity.
We have allowed conditions to develop whereby on the one hand the farmer has an abundance and then must go and beg for the right to sell his commodity. So far as the attitude of the government is concerned, in refusing to consider in any way, shape or form any deal which would be on a mutually advantageous level, I think that is a very nearsighted attitude. It is desirable and absolutely essential that in our modern world we think in terms of creating sales up to a sensible and reasonable amount. If it were not that we are living in a world which is definitely conscious of the credit system our economy would not have reached a level of $26,400 million. Those who manufacture television sets, refrigerators and that kind of thing do so in the expectation that people will mortgage their future incomes to buy those articles on credit. If we are going to sell our wheat or anything else we must think more or less in those terms. We must be ready to sell some of our commodities on a credit basis.
I think this is really a backwash of faulty techniques in our fiscal policy. We have allowed our fiscal policy to take on a lot of dry rot. If we are to consider this bill on its merits I think we should follow the suggestion made by my colleague and send it to the committee after second reading. We could then take advantage of the collective thinking and good judgment of the people of Canada who are so vitally interested. The government would be able to listen to those people and if this legislation is not what the people want it could be modified without the government in my opinion losing face at all. In fact I think they would become more or less heroes as a result. If a man makes a mistake and is ready to admit it and tries to remedy it, he is doing the right thing. I urge the government in its mature wisdom to allow this bill to go to a committee where it can be given the acid test. Then whatever seems to be the sensible thing to be done can be done. We would be doing what the people of Canada want. If that were done the government could take credit for having the courage to take one more look at the matter in an effort to come up with the right answer.
I think it is a pity that the government has adopted the attitude that they will not permit this bill to go before the committee. It is certainly not in the interests of the agricultural industry when they refuse to do that. I would urge that they give one more look and agree to the proposal made by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch).

Mr. Speaker, if the eyebrows of the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Dickey) rise slightly when he sees me taking part in this debate, let me assure him at once that I do not intend to go into any detailed statistical analysis of the wheat marketing problem or the detailed pros and cons of the legislation before the house. I feel that the situation as it affects the farmers has been adequately set forth by those of my colleagues who are much closer to it.
I say at once that my reason for rising to take part briefly in this debate is to say that in my opinion the subject matter of this bill is of concern to a much broader section of the people of Canada than the producers of wheat in the three prairie provinces. I think the government should realize that this particular piece of legislation and the effect it is going to have upon the welfare, not only of the farmers but of many of the rest of the people of Canada, are under much closer review than they may perhaps realize. As most hon. members know, in the constituency I represent there are a good many industrial workers. I want to suggest that among the industrial workers of this country there is a growing realization that the situation of the Canadian farmers and their own situation are much more closely parallel than they may perhaps have realized a few years ago.
Perhaps I might give one or two illustrations of that fact. Not so long ago, since the beginning of the present session of this house, as a matter of fact, I was invited to speak at a public meeting in one of the large industrial centres of Canada. The audience was composed largely of people who were industrial workers, and the topic which it had been suggested I might discuss was the new Unemployment Insurance Act. Of course, if the Minister of Labour had been there it would perhaps have been a more interesting discussion than we had. But the point I wish to make is that when we came to a question period at the end of the meeting, rather to my surprise the questions that were asked of me were not in the main directed to the Unemployment Insurance Act but to the situation in respect to the wheat surplus in Canada and the policies the government was formulating to deal with it.
I mention that because I think it serves to illustrate the point I am trying to make, that this is a measure of concern not only to my colleagues who come from agricultural constituencies in the prairie provinces but also to a great many people in a great many parts of Canada. In my district I meet from time to time quite a large number of people

who at one time or another have been prairie fanners. Where do I meet those people? Do I meet them driving around in the Cadillacs about which the Minister of Trade and Commerce was talking? Do I meet them frequenting posh resorts? No; I meet those people working in the sawmills and logging camps of Vancouver island.
That fact illustrates another point I should like to emphasize, that basically the situation of the agricultural producers of this country and that of the industrial producers of this country are the same. If the industrial workers were faced with the kind of situation which has been adequately described, where their pay cheques had been drastically reduced, and then they found at the end of the week or month they were not in a position to collect the other half of their pay cheques but were having suggested to them that they should go to the bank and get a government guaranteed loan at 5 per cent, their position would be rather similar to that in which the government is proposing to place the farmers of the western prairies by this legislation.
I felt I should like to take part briefly in this debate to emphasize the growing realization among the industrial workers of this country that legislation that is inadequate for the farmers is also going to have bad results as far as they are concerned. In considering whether or not the amendment now before the house on this legislation should be accepted, members in all parts of the house-not only those who come from agricultural constituencies in the prairie provinces but also those who may represent industrial constituencies in eastern Canada or other parts of the country-should realize that the eyes of many of the people of Canada are upon the actions of the government and the inadequacies of the measure it is now proposing to bring in.

Mr. Speaker, I can imagine that some hon. members may have in their minds the question as to how many grain farms there are in Winnipeg North Centre. I think it is generally known that the answer is none. Nevertheless, I doubt that any member of this house has any greater claim to speak on this matter than has the member for Winnipeg North Centre, in view of the list of head offices that are located within the bounds of my constituency.
Within the boundaries of Winnipeg North Centre may be found the head office of the Canadian wheat board. Also in my constituency is the Winnipeg grain exchange. We also have the head office of the board of grain commissioners. There is also the 67509-80
Grain
head office of the wheat pool. The Manitoba federation of agriculture and co-operation has its head office in Winnipeg North Centre, as does the Manitoba farmers' union. I might also point out that every carload of grain that comes from anywhere west of Winnipeg headed toward the lakehead, whether on the Canadian National or the Canadian Pacific railway, comes through the constituency of Winnipeg North Centre.
So in our riding we have a real interest in agricultural matters. In addition to that, as my friend and neighbour the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) pointed out a few days ago, all of us in the west recognize the important place that agriculture holds in our economy. We recognize that what is good for the farmers of western Canada is good for western Canada as a whole, and we feel that anything that is unfair and unjust to the farmers of western Canada is an injustice to western Canada as a whole.
Therefore I rise for just a few minutes to indicate my support of the amendment moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Johnson), and my opposition to the bill, the second reading of which is now before the house.
Reference has already been made to the "Press Conference" program, which many of us saw and heard on television last evening, when the gentleman being interviewed by the press, under the chairmanship of Professor Kenneth MacNaught of Winnipeg, was Mr. Harper Prowse, the Liberal leader in Alberta. We were interested in the way in which he was questioned about this legislation. He said at first it was his personal view that cash advances would be better, but then he tried to get off into a discussion of the bank loan legislation and tried to find something good about it. We were interested in the way in which one of the newspapermen put Mr. Prowse squarely on the spot and asked him what his own personal view was. He said that in his personal view cash advances would be preferable.
However, in the attempt that he did make to justify the bank loan way of dealing with this matter I thought he made one of the most telling arguments against the legislation now before the house. He put it something like this, if my memory from seeing and hearing the program serves me well; that one of the desirable features of the bank loan way of dealing with the problem was that only those farmers who desperately needed money would go to the banks and get it. As I say, that was about the only argument he advanced for it.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that that is as much as to say to a worker in an industry

Grain
that at the end of the week or two weeks, whatever his pay period is, he should not take his wages unless he really desperately needs them at that particular time. That is as much as to say to a member of parliament or a cabinet minister that at the end of the month he should not go to the pay office and collect his monthly cheque unless at that time he really needs it.
In our economy, in our society, Mr. Speaker, it is a basic principle that when people have done the work they were expected to do in connection with their job, occupation or profession they are entitled at the end of that period to their wages or pay for what they have done. It is our contention that the farmers of western Canada, having produced a bumper crop in 1955, are entitled without further delay to a return for what they have done and they are entitled to it as a matter of right, without having to go to the banks and borrow a portion of what they need at 5 per cent interest.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that last night Mr. Harper Prowse, in his feeble attempt to defend this legislation, pointed very clearly to what is wrong with it. We take the position, as I have indicated, that the farmers of western Canada, having done their year's work, should not now be told that the only way they can get any money is by going to the banks and paying interest, it being understood that they will not do so unless they desperately need it. That they need cash we know very well, but whether or not their need is desperate they are entitled to it. We feel that the only way that entitlement can be expressed under present conditions is by means of cash advances in respect of grain stored on the farms which the farmers of western Canada are prepared to deliver.
So, Mr. Speaker, we feel that this matter should not be pushed through in the form in which the bill is now before the house, but rather that the subject matter of the bill should be referred to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization so that interested bodies can appear before that committee and so that further consideration can be given to the matter.
The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce objected to the amendment of my colleague, the hon. member for Kin-dersley, by saying that if this amendment were carried it would mean the defeat of the bill and would prevent a bill like this being introduced again this session. I feel that argument should be dealt with at least for a minute or two. First may I say that so far as we are concerned we are not frightened by

the charge that the carrying of this amendment would mean the defeat of the bill. After all, we are trying to defeat it and that is fine. But, Mr. Speaker, we have left the door open for even such a bill as this to be presented again to the house if, after consideration by a committee, that committee having had a chance to hear responsible organizations, a recommendation to that effect is made by the committee to the house.
We are not on a point of order so I am not going to pick up Beauchesne and read it, but I would remind the minister that citation 663 of Beauchesne, third edition, makes it clear that these motions that deny the "now" reading for the second time of a bill do not prevent a motion being made for second reading at a later time. All this amendment does is to deny the reading at this particular time. It is still possible, if the committee were so to recommend, to reintroduce legislation even along these lines at this same session.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, we feel that if the committee were given a chance to go into this matter thoroughly, if the committee were given a chance to hear the various organizations and get it straightened out for all who can hear as to what the farmers of western Canada want, that committee given a free hand would not recommend the reintroduction of a bill of this kind. We are satisfied that if the committee went into the matter thoroughly and heard representations from organizations representing the western farmers it would propose something much more akin to what we in this group have been advocating, namely cash advances to the farmers in respect of grain stored on the farm.
Naturally we have all been interested in the remarks made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce with regard to the legislation, and also with regard to the course the debate has taken. The minister does not like quotations of what he has said unless they are picked straight out of Hansard, so I will try to avoid offending him by putting words in his mouth that he did not use. However, I think it is pretty clear that he is annoyed that the debate is taking so long.
I am going to say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that I think one of the reasons he is annoyed at the length of time this debate is taking is that he has not any effective club to hold over those of us who are opposing the legislation. At times there are measures before the house which are grossly inadequate and which we on the opposition side of the house oppose in the hope they will be improved. In circumstances such as those the

Grain
government can sometimes hold over us the club that unless we let even such inadequate legislation go through its benefits will not reach those tor whom the benefits are intended.
But the Minister of Trade and Commerce knows as well as we do that any benefits that might accrue to individual farmers from this legislation have already been obtained by those farmers. If the debate goes on:r another day, another week, or is put off to the end of June it does not make a particle of difference to a single farmer in western Canada. Any farmer who would be able to borrow money from the banks, up to $1,500 at 5 per cent, after the passing of this bill can borrow that money now. In fact, the likelihood is that all who would take advantage of it have already done so. So the minister has no club over us in our opposition to this bill.
I mention that not just to remind the minister of the annoyance he is feeling, but also because the fact that it would make no difference whether or not this bill was passed emphasizes how utterly lacking in value it is. Just suppose this bill did not get passed.
the government in saying to the farmers, "This is all you get." I could recite the old saying that the good is the enemy of the best, but it would not be appropriate because there is nothing good about this legislation. The trouble with legislation of this kind being passed is that, in the government's mind at any rate, it blocks consideration of anything else. I therefore hope that, even if we have to have it by means of a government majority, there will be a strong opposition to this bill from this side of the house that will let the government know that so far as we are concerned this is not the end of dealing with the problem of achieving justice and fairness for the farmers of western Canada.
Mr. Speaker, there is before the house an' amendment moved by my colleague the hon. member for Kindersley which, as I have indicated, has our full support. As my colleague the hon. member for Dauphin suggested earlier today, we still feel that the government might do well to let a free vote be taken on this amendment and give such members on the government side as wish to do so the opportunity to support that amendment as well.
Would any farmer in western Canada suffer? Not one. Would any bank suffer? No. No bank has lent any money to any farmer on the strength of the letters from the Minister of Finance unless it was sure it was going to get its money back anyway. Hence if the bill does not pass, nobody suffers.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce said one time, "What are we debating about? There is nothing to debate about". Maybe he is right and there is nothing to debate about. There is no value to the bill at all. If it does not pass there is no change in the situation. But, Mr. Speaker, what happens if this bill passes is that the government is in a position to say to the farmers of western Canada that, between this and one other piece of legislation, "Here is the program; we are doing nothing more."
In that respect I may say this, and I say it frankly but kindly. I was disappointed in the vote at the resolution stage of our friends to the right and to the left of us, and I am highly pleased to know that on the vote that may take place shortly they are going to vote with us on our amendment and also against the second reading of the bill. I plead with them to stay with us in opposing this measure down the line.
This is one of those occasions, however, when I wish it were possible for us to move a different kind of amendment. I should like to have just a moment, Your Honour, to read a few sentences from May's thirteenth edition in order to indicate the kind of amendment that I think would have been even more appropriate than the amendment moved by my colleague the hon. member for Kindersley. I refer to page 394 of May's Parliamentary Practice, thirteenth edition, where I read:
In more ancient times bills were treated with even greater ignominy. On the 23rd January, 1562/3, a bill was rejected and ordered to be tom; so, also, on the 17th March, 1620/21, Sir Edward Coke moved "to have the bill tom in the house;" and it is entered that the bill was accordingly "rejected and tom, without one negative." I used that merely as an illustration of the idea that prevails amongst some hon. members. Yesterday I said "scandalous" when reference was made to what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said concerning those who were so well off, giving the impression that most farmers in the west were in the happy position of that particular man. I say that was pernicious because it would give so many people in the house who come from other provinces an altogether false idea concerning conditions on the prairie provinces.
I hope I have made my point. May I say to the members who come from provinces other than the three prairie provinces that if you could get together a complete account of all the grain which has been produced in those three prairie provinces since 1890 and sold for good, solid foreign exchange, you would be astounded at the service those provinces had rendered to the Dominion of Canada. They provide foreign exchange because that grain can always be sold for foreign exchange, whether or not it does the farmer who produced the wheat any good.
Now, I have not the figures compiled to indicate how great is the debt that Canada owes to her wheat growers in the three prairie provinces, merely on the matter of foreign exchange alone. I am sure everybody in this house is deeply perturbed by reason of the fact we are so dangerously indebted to the United States. We have an adverse trade balance every single year. This is simply putting our necks in a noose which will ultimately strangle us to death. This is enough to show you how serious it is to have production which results in foreign exchange for the advantage of this nation.
Well, that is just the first point. I would urge hon. members to forget entirely all this nonsense which has been given to them concerning the rank and file of farmers in those three prairie provinces living in luxury, riding off to California, Florida and that sort of thing. I have grown up and lived all my life amongst those farmers. They have
Grain
never been able to go off to California or Florida or anywhere else. They have to have their noses right to the grindstone, just as my poor father had his. He farmed all the time I knew him, and he was injured by the rise and fall of prices as a result of trading on the open market just as tens of thousands of others were. We were very glad, therefore, when the wheat board was established.
There is another matter with which I hope hon. members can impress themselves. In the year 1946-no doubt the Minister of Trade and Commerce exercised a very powerful influence-this government permitted the steel companies to advance the price of steel by $5 per ton. That act looked rather simple at the time. I do not know whether the minister foresaw what a potentially catastrophic thing that was, but he must have agreed to it. What happened? Everyone whose memory goes back to that time will recall that the steel workers of Canada in the various mills struck for their share of that $5 per ton. They continued that strike for 82 days, and the industrial relations committee of this house heard discussions on that strike for many of those days. The result of the whole thing was that by the time we were finished with that experience the prices of practically everything in the Dominion of Canada had been forced upward.
Was this inflation? No, it was not inflation. Inflation is a rise in price which results from a scarcity of goods. Anyone who thinks he can challenge that statement can get up on the floor and do it right now. Was there any shortage of steel which caused the increase in price? Not a bit of it. Was there any shortage of labour which caused the rise in the wages? Not a bit of it. The result of that increase by $5 per ton in the price of steel and the strike of the men following it was an over-all increase in prices. But it had nothing at all to do with inflation, one way or another.
It being six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I would ask you to let me discontinue my remarks until after the recess.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of personal privilege. This afternoon a verbal hassle occurred with respect to an unnamed hon. member from British Columbia who was opposed to the wheat legislation. I know that the hon. members for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more), Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) and Acadia (Mr. Quelch) certainly wanted to be perfectly fair in connection with this matter, and I want at this time to be perfectly fair, too.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, there is no secrecy attached to this matter at all. Although some confusion exists, the whole thing is in Hansard. I made the statement referred to on the 16th day of January, at page 143. I then quoted Votes and Proceedings for January 12, as follows:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure for the payment of carrying costs of temporary wheat reserves owned by the Canadian wheat board in respect of board stocks of wheat in excess of one hundred and seventy-eight million bushels at the commencement of a crop year, such payment to be made to the board by the Minister of Finance out of the consolidated revenue fund.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, there are two bills dealing with wheat. From what I have just quoted it is most obvious that I was referring specifically to Bill No. 83 and not to Bill No. 82 which is now before the house. As far as Bill No. 82 is concerned I wish to assure you, sir, that I am 100 per cent in favour of the bill.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe (Port Arthur) for the second reading of Bill No. 82, to provide for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Johnson (Kindersley).

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. MacDougall) was here in order to put his case before the house with adequate clarity. His case merely strengthens the position I was taking. This bill which we are

now discussing can hardly be of any value whatsoever to the farmers in western Canada as has been abundantly shown in the debate up to the present time.
The other bill which is yet coming along, which provides for the payment by the government of a certain amount of storage on grain which has accumulated in the country by reason of the fact that the government is unable to dispose of that grain abroad, will be of real value to everyone who has grain in storage. That is the bill which the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard should support, because it is one which will help the farmer, but it is the one which he opposes. The bill which will burden the farmer with a great deal of debt and which will destroy the farmer is the bill he is willing to see go through.
Before the recess I was indicating that I thought there are a great many people in the country, altogether too many in the provinces of Ontario, British Columbia and the maritimes, who fail to understand the true situation in respect of the wheat growers of the three prairie provinces, and who are therefore quite wrongly led with respect to the prosperity which is supposed to exist on the prairies.
I was pointing out that the wheat growers of the three prairie provinces have done a great service to the nation through the years, from 1890 on, for example, by raising grain which has invariably been sold for exceedingly valuable foreign exchange, which has helped Canada to keep herself above water in the payment of her international commitments.
I was also, pointing out just before six o'clock that a very serious blunder was made by the government in Ottawa in granting the steel producers an increase of $5 a ton in the price of steel in April, 1946. This was done by the government including the present Minister of Trade and Commerce and the present Minister of Agriculture. They cannot possibly escape the responsibility for having done this. In doing this they were backed by their party. I heard not a member dissenting. The responsibility is shared by a large percentage of the people in the Progressive Conservative party, these people representing all the provinces of Canada. There is no way in the world whereby the provinces I referred to, Ontario, British Columbia and the maritimes, can escape the indirect responsibility for that $5 advance in the price of steel.
That advance in the price of steel has put the farmers in the three prairie provinces at a disadvantage the seriousness of which

Grain
no one in the country begins to realize. In large measure it has meant disaster to the prairie farmers. The only way they could have avoided disaster would have been to dispose of their grain at good prices, which they have not been able to do. I propose to go into that matter just a little more fully in the time that remains at my disposal.
Let us not forget, first of all, that when the advance in the price of steel of $5 a ton was made the steel workers demanded and got their share of the $5. They went on strike for 82 days. At the end of the strike they won their point, which gave them an increase in wages, and this resulted in an increase in wages for virtually every section of the labouring class in the Dominion of Canada, thereby forcing up the cost of Canada's production.
This had nothing whatsoever to do with inflation. It was a forcing up of prices, a price manipulation. At the same time the increase in the price of steel forced up the price of every commodity into the processing of which the matter of steel entered, which includes, of course, almost every industry in Canada.
If we can only get that clearly in our minds we will begin to see one of the great causes of the trouble which today exists among farmers in the three prairie provinces. So many people nowadays are saying that this rise in price which we have sustained is inflation. Every hon. member in this house should know, and if he does not know it is a reflection on him, that the rise in price had nothing to do with inflation. It had nothing to do with the amount of money in circulation, and it had nothing to do with the shortage of goods. There were plenty of goods whenever any one of the increases in price occurred, and it is impossible for anyone to show there was not. Consequently there was no justification whatsoever for the increase in price except that the increase in the cost of production had come about through manipulation and not through a shortage of goods.
As I said a moment ago, this increase in the price of steel is at the bottom of the major cause of the difficulty confronting the farmers at the present time, which is a difficulty I feel everyone in Canada would be glad to help the western farmers out of if the truth were known.
Let us see what has been the result of these increases in the price of steel. The Financial Post in a survey shows that 25 corporations which do business with farmers increased their average profit after taxes by 402 per cent between 1946 and 1954. This
means in effect that the government by permitting the $5 increase opened a back gate and turned into the Queen's garden a whole herd of hogs that had no respect at all for the welfare of the people; they just grabbed and gouged every single cent they possibly could and that herd of hogs is practically entirely made up of these 25 corporations. Those corporations were getting plenty of money with which to carry on during the war and they made good profits; but after the war, through this manipulation of the $5 a ton increase, they were simply allowed to go freely at will into the pockets of the Canadian consumers to rob them of every cent of which it was within their power to rob them.
The figures I have given indicate in some measure the result of that situation. These figures which I have given hon. members will be able to verify by consulting page 7 of the submission to the government of Canada by the interprovincial farm union council, which was presented on February 16, 1956. Remember that this document is quoting a survey conducted by the Financial Post.
Let me repeat once more that that is the cause of the difficulty which is ruining the farmers in the three prairie provinces. In the main those farmers rely upon grain, especially wheat, as the means whereby they can pay the excessive costs which have been brought about by the profits these companies have taken. Anything which affects the price or the ultimate value which the farmer derives from wheat will put him under an unbearable pressure financially.
We can consider this matter of purchasing power in another way, and I am going to cite some other figures for hon. members to contemplate to indicate the amount of money taken by these corporations from the people of Alberta.

Cash advances to farmers were the subject of an amendment moved to the address in reply to the speech from the throne, which amendment was fully debated and voted upon by the house. It is difficult in criticizing this bill not to indicate a preference for cash advances, but if in trying to make that point the hon. member refers to the ill effects of an increase in the price of steel; if he refers to that particular factor and others in the same category during the greater part of his speech and refers only indirectly to the measure now before us, then I do not think it makes for orderly debate.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not sure in what position I am now standing. Do I conclude my speech or may I continue?

I bow to your ruling. Maybe I am not able to detect relevancy, but if it were proposed that advances should be given to farmers the first thing I would want to know would be how badly off are they. That is just exactly what the minister has been trying to argue all the way through.
rMr. Blackmore.]
He and the Minister of Agriculture have been arguing along those lines. It is as simple as A, B, C.
Then the next thing I would want to know would be what caused them to be that way, how it was that they were so badly off. Was it because they have not been good managers? Was it because of any fault of their own? The figures I intend to advance show that it was not any cause of their own making.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

This is no laughing matter. Every farmer who buys a combine or any machine whatsoever has his cost of production increased by the increase in the price of steel. Everything which causes his cost of production to rise creates an additional cost-price squeeze. There is no doubt about that. Under the circumstances I would say that it would be absolutely impossible to discuss this amendment with greater relevancy than I am doing at the present time. That is perhaps contrary to the opinion of Mr. Speaker and I bow to your ruling, but I am quite sure that is the way the majority of farmers see it.
I was going to give two sets of figures which are very brief but which are most enlightening. If after I have given these figures Mr. Speaker feels that I should discontinue this discussion, I shall gladly do so. I was going to give figures to indicate what had been taken away from the farmers and people of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba during the period 1940-45, when we were under price controls and when apparently the companies were getting along all right, in contrast to what was taken away during the period 1946-54, when the hogs were loose and the herd was running in every direction.
During the period 1940-45 those companies took out of the hands of the consumers in Alberta $320,041,005, but during the period 1946-54 they took from the pockets of the people of Alberta $2,877,463,723. If you want to find out why the farmers in Alberta, who had to absorb the greatest proportion of the impact of that situation, are in difficulty, it is so plain that even the minister should see it.
In Saskatchewan during the period 1940-45 they took away from the people $392,639,284, whereas in the period 1946-54 they took away $2,723,168,516. It is said by the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the farmers of Saskatchewan

are not in bad condition. One would have to be blind not to see the impact of that situation.
In Manitoba during the period 1940-45 these companies took out of the pockets of the people $293,639,220, whereas in the period 1946-54 they took out $2,220,455,357. Do you wonder that the farming people in those provinces are in difficult circumstances? What would you do about it?
Before I go any further, let me point out once again that the responsibility for the incursion of the hogs into the Queen's garden lies on the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the people with him in the cabinet who made the decision to permit that $5 advance in steel. It lies on the people who supported that motion, who came very largely from Ontario, Quebec, the maritime provinces and British Columbia. There is no way of escaping that responsibility. The responsibility for this difficulty in which we find our prairie farmers lies on the government that is now in power.
The question now is, what are we going to do about it? I am not going to prescribe now what has to be done about it but, whenever it is suggested that the western farmers need advances or that they need payment for storage on farms or in elevators, I do urge upon every hon. member of this house from every province outside the prairies to bear these facts strictly in mind.

In the light of all that, I think we ought to set the record straight. The other day the hon. member was quite concerned about setting the record straight. In fairness I suggest that we ought to make it quite clear where the government of Saskatchewan stands on this question of bank loans. Hon. I. C. Nollet, minister of agriculture in the province of Saskatchewan, made this statement:
I supported the wheat board payment proposal on behalf of the government of Saskatchewan as the fairest and most practical way to deal with the situation.
Since the farmer has so far carried the entire load of storage and marketing costs and is now faced with lower prices, he should not be compelled to borrow money from a bank on grain in the bin which through no fault of his own he is unable to market. We feel that advance cash payments on farm-stored grain must become an established part of wheat board marketing, . . .
This view has been endorsed by the Saskatchewan legislature and has been brought to the attention of the Right Hon. C. D. Howe on several occasions ... I again brought this matter to the attention of the federal government at the conference.
It was disappointing to find the federal government had already decided that regular lending institutions would be called upon to meet the immediate situation, rather than employing an advance payment plan.
Those are the exact words of the minister of agriculture in the province of Saskatchewan. Yet the other day the hon. member for Rosthern made a direct statement to the effect that the interpretation which he placed on the Saskatoon conference had been endorsed by the Saskatchewan government.
While we are on this point, Mr. Speaker, may I say this. I just wonder what organizations at the Saskatoon conference had wanted to take bank loans. I wonder whether the hon. member for Rosthern could inform hon. members of the house what organizations at that conference asked for bank loans. Was it the wheat pool? Was it the Saskatchewan

farmers' union? The hon. member for Ros-thern is not able to name one Saskatchewan farm organization which at that conference came out for bank loans.
What happened was this. When the delegation came to Ottawa, in an effort to present a unanimous report they were a little bit vague as to the manner in which this policy was to be put into effect. But here is the interesting point. The other day the hon. member for Rosthern was reading into Hansard the resolution passed at the Saskatoon conference and, as appears at page 1158 of Hansard, he read into the record the following:
While the principle of cash advances on farm-stored grain was unanimously endorsed by the organizations present at the conference various proposals were offered on the mechanics of making these advances.
Then the hon. member went on to quote four alternative methods of putting the scheme into effect, one of which was that of bank loans. The hon. member selected the proposal which suited his convenience, the one of which he approves and of which the government approves, namely that of bank loans; and he says because the conference were not specific they obviously meant bank loans. But bank loans were only one of four proposals put forward. Then by the same token he argues that because they did not say cash advances on farm-stored grain paid by the wheat board, they are therefore opposed to cash advances paid by the wheat board.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that that is entirely a matter of the interpretation of each individual person who reads these resolutions. However, I draw to the attention of the house the fact that the hon. member chose the one alternative which suited his purpose, the one alternative on which this government had decided. Because the delegation made a mistake, in an effort to present a unanimous front-because they made the mistake of not being too specific-they fell into the error of having a wrong interpretation placed on their recommendations by the government and by the hon. member for Rosthern.
If it is logical to say that the delegation asked for bank loans, I suggest that it is just as logical to say that they asked for cash advances paid by the wheat board. The very fact that they were not too specific can in no way be_ used as an argument in favour of the legislation now before this house. I think that is a matter that is quite serious. The other day the hon. member for Rosthern, several times-and I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)

got to his feet on the occasion on a point of order-as reported at page 1160 of Hansard said:

Some reference has been made to television, and I suggest that the hon. member take exceptional care, because in making statements from the public platform one is not accorded the protection of a soundproof broadcasting booth in a television studio.
I have referred to the speeches made in this house by Liberal members from my own province. I have gone through them very carefully in an attempt to find out what reasons they are advancing for supporting the legislation before us. I have not found a single reason put forward. I am wondering why they are supporting it if it is not because they are toeing the party line.
Some reference has been made to the leader of the Liberal party in Alberta who appeared on "Press Conference" last night. He stated in no uncertain terms that Liberal fortunes were not too good at the moment in the west in view of the agriculture policy being put forward by this government. He went on to say some glowing things about his own province, but when the reporters asked of him how he thought the Liberal party in western Canada was faring in the light of the agriculture policy being put forth by the government, he hesitated somewhat and then began to damn it with faint praise.
I referred earlier to the attitude of the leader of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan.

Grain
Initially he had the same reaction as hon. members of the C.C.F. group, that the legislation was completely inadequate and was not going to do the job which we felt had to be done.
We have an amendment before the house which, if it passes, will send this bill to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization. I am at a loss to understand why the government will not accept this amendment. We recall that the other night the Minister of Trade and Commerce issued a threat -perhaps on reconsideration I could properly describe it as a bluff-that if we were not good boys he was going to put off this legislation until June. If that is his attitude, I am curious as to why the Liberals do not vote for this amendment and send it to the committee. Then this bill would not come before the house for some time. If the minister is interested in putting off this matter we have opened the door for him. All he and his Liberal followers have to do is vote for the C.C.F. amendment to refer this matter to the committee. After the committee has discussed it and after the various farm organizations have had an opportunity to make their representations, the matter can be brought back before the house.
I do not believe anyone need feel too much concern over the fact that this matter is being discussed. It is being discussed thoroughly because the government has not accepted this amendment. When we find hon. members reading resolutions which are quite clear to all who wish to read them properly, and interpreting them in such a fashion as to completely defeat not only the intent but the spirit of those resolutions, then I think those people have a right to clarify their position. Some other members have mentioned that if we were to refer this bill to a committee it would enable the farmers in western Canada to make their representations. They would then be in a position to let the government supporters know how they feel on these matters.
By the way, Mr. Speaker, I hope that perhaps the Liberal members from Saskatchewan have a little clearer understanding of the problems out west since their meeting with the farm union delegation. I trust that they paid strict attention to the representations made, and I hope they will have had some effect on the way those members are going to vote on this particular measure.
We have had arguments advanced as to why we should support the legislation. We have had arguments against the legislation. But I suggest, looking at it from an objective point of view, that if hon. members

were to go back to the record of this debate and draw up a balance sheet of the arguments in favour of and against this legislation there would be no question as to where the bulk of the evidence would lie.
We have had speeches by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Agriculture and private members supporting the government, but we have not had any discussion about the impact this legislation will have on the prairies. The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Bryson) yesterday put before this house certain figures to indicate the effect this legislation would have on the small farmers on the prairies. He referred specifically to farmers with a quarter section, a half section and three quarters of a section, and indicated the extent to which those people could obtain loans.
We have had no discussion from government supporters. They have not considered the implication of the legislation. They have made up their minds it is good for the people out west and they are going to force it on us whether or not we like it. In my judgment that is the best reason why this house should vote for the amendment to refer this bill to the committee on agriculture and colonization, where it belongs.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a long silence in connection with this measure does not indicate by any means that I am not interested in what is before the house. I think it would be fair to say that this condition we are trying to remedy did not come upon us in the last few months. It has been with us now for three or four years. Farm income has been steadily dropping. We are now asked to put the rubber stamp of approval on a hurry-up measure that is already in operation. As I recall it, the minister said that practically all the loans that are going to be made under this legislation have been made. Since we have had this decline in farm income for some time, surely we should not have had to rush in with something in the middle of November and now come here as a group to put on the rubber stamp of approval.
I had one other thing in mind when I rose. Since there is a group of people from the farm union here, I should like to see someone on the government side stand up and explain why this bill should not go to the agriculture committee. It is all right for somepne to get up in the house and flatly say, "No", but I think we should know why the government take that stand. I should like to have someone on the government side explain that to the house.

That is about all I have to say on this measure at this time. I may have something else to say when the bill goes to committee. I would urge the government to explain to us, Mr. Speaker, exactly why this bill could not go to the committee after second reading, and why they would not give an undertaking to have that done.

speechtext: Fairy tales.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
There is not an hon. member opposite who will suggest for one moment that there are not many hon. members on the other side who have expressed their disapproval of this bill but who will not express it here.
We have indicated quite clearly that we sought to have provision made that would in fact bring relief to the farmers of western Canada at a time when they need cash and need it desperately in the midst of all this immense accumulation of grain. The explanation we have had that this is only because of a succession of good crops is simply an evasion of the reality which must be faced and which this government has not faced.
When we were at the resolution stage I indicated that we hoped the government would still bring down legislation which, if they still insisted on bringing this in, would combine with it the provision for cash payments for farm-stored grain. We did not have the legislation before us. We had been told that the government was going to introduce legislation to provide for loans by the banks.
Of course the government acted in the way it ordinarily acts in relation to parliament. We had urged that we have a special session last fall to deal with this. That would have been the proper way to deal with this subject. Before this government told the banks to go ahead and make loans, no matter what their majority is, there should at least have been a sufficient measure of apparent respect for the independence of its members not to assume in advance that they would necessarily rubber-stamp what the government did. We should have been called together here to pass upon legislation of this kind. Had we been brought together, we could then have urged from the very beginning the kind of legislation we think would deal with this situation.
It will be recalled that when we indicated at the stage when the motion was before us that it was expedient to introduce legislation, we were pressing then for a broadening of the legislation, a widening of its application to embrace payments on farm-stored grain. We supported that resolution simply for the purpose of proceeding and permitting the government to consider what legislation it would bring in. It now brings in legislation that is similar in all respects to an act which over and over again they have

told us was no good. This bill before us is almost identical with the bill introduced in 1951 under the title of the Prairie Grain Producers' Interim Financing Act, 1951. Over and over again we have been told by the government that this act was ineffective.
Surely we had reason to expect that we were not simply going to have a repetition of an ineffective act. knows perfectly well what is meant by a quota book. It is described in the bill as a permit book. It is known to the farmers as a quota book and is known to the Minister of Trade and Commerce as such.
It is typical of the way in which this debate has been conducted that an attempt should be made to create any suggestion that the minister was not fully aware of what a quota book is. A quota book is well understood by the farmers of western Canada as meaning the permit book described in the bill. One of the results of that endorsement of the loan in the permit book is that the farmer cannot then deliver his grain to the elevator and therefore he not only has the problem of not being able to deliver his grain but he has an entry on his quota book or permit book, if the minister prefers that term, which prevents him carrying out the very transaction that is going to make it easier for him to repay the loan.
It is a typical achievement of the draftsmanship of this government that they should have a provision of that kind. This legislation is a little worse than the 1951 act, but not much. That of course was the act that they thought was such an unsatisfactory act. We have urged the government to reconsider this legislation. We have urged the government to provide in any event for cash payments, and it is perfectly clear that this bill, which deals with the permit book, to use the name the minister prefers, could easily have provided also for cash payments in relation to that same permit book.
It could have been done. It has not been done. The motion that was made by way of amendment on behalf of the Progressive Conservative party was ruled out of order. An amendment was then moved by a representative of the C.C.F. party and we supported that amendment.
Now we come to the bill itself. The cash advances that we have sought certainly are in no way contemplated or provided under the legislation now before us. On top of that is the attitude of the government in dealing with this whole matter. We have had no real explanation why the government was not prepared to consider this, except some suggestions of dealing with the permit book as we have argued. There was a typical example in the debate yesterday of the way in which this matter has been dealt with. The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) was asking that the bill be referred to a committee and, as reported at page 1210 of Hansard for February 15, the hon. member for Acadia,

That, Mr. Speaker, is typical of the whole attitude of the government-no attempt to explain to the members of the house, no attempt to explain why our very reasonable proposals should not be carried out.
As has already been pointed out tonight, if the subject matter of the bill had been referred to a committee then the whole thing could have been examined with representatives of the various farm groups present and there would have been an opportunity to find out firsthand from the farmers themselves exactly what it was they wanted. In any event, we now find ourselves simply with the bill, a bill that the government described as unsatisfactory in its 1951 form and a bill which, now that we have it before us, is definitely more unsatisfactory today.
The arrogance of the government in relation to this has simply been a further expression of their contempt of parliament. They have been unwilling to listen to arguments. They have brought down a bill they themselves said was bad, and they have made it worse by the revisions that are in it. We shall certainly vote against the bill on second reading.

Then in the speech from the throne closing the session on January 31, 1945, there was this:
As a further safeguard of a basic standard of living, provision was made at the present session for floors under the prices of farm and fish products. These measures insure two great primary industries against the hazard of a collapse of markets or prices after the war.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the farmers in all parts of Canada accepted the fact that price controls were in the public interest. While the farmers had 10 years of rough going in all parts of Canada, the manufacturers had been able to convince the Minister of Trade and Commerce that they should operate on a cost plus basis. The minister yielded to pressure and removed the 5 per cent limit, so that the sky was the limit during the war for those who were taking contracts for munitions. But those who were producing food for our own nation and for our overseas customers were forced to produce on a cost minus basis. I submit that the commitment made by the Prime Minister of Canada when he went on the air on December 4, 1943, should not be forgotten.
I hoped the members from the prosperous areas of central Ontario and Montreal would have more consideration for the farmers on the back concessions of Quebec, Ontario and the maritimes, whose position is similar to the position of all other farmers. It so happens that this particular piece of legislation permits us to bring our problems to the only place where we can discuss them, to this parliament.
I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that while we are speaking about our problems we do not suggest for a moment that the potato growers in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, the fruit farmers and vegetable farmers in western Canada do not have problems which are just as real for them. But those problems are not going to be solved by the members of the cabinet who are so tired and so out of touch with the problems in the different parts of the country that they fail to consider the statistics made available by the bureau of statistics.
As it is ten o'clock, I would move the adjournment of the debate.

Just before I put the motion, I should like to tell the hon. member that in trying to appreciate what may be relevant in this debate, I find it very difficult to understand why one should be allowed to review the position of agriculture in the 10 provinces of Canada when we are dealing now with the grain producers. I will ask the hon. member to take into consideration the fact

that several speakers in this debate already have made several points to prove that the condition of the western farmer at the moment is not as good as it has been represented by some members of the government.
Perhaps now he should deal with the principle of this bill and not spend all his time discussing a problem which is, of course, one of great importance and interest, but which there will be other opportunities to discuss. There is the first item of the Department of Agriculture and some items in the Department of Trade and Commerce on which the whole subject of agriculture will probably be opened up for discussion. The hon. member has reviewed the position of agriculture on February 16, and he will want to review it
again on February 29, etc. I hope the hon. member appreciates what I am saying and recognizes the validity of some of the points I am stressing at the moment.
